The idealizer of the semigroup of stable polynomials

Michał Kudra Note: Partially supported by Sheng grant no. 2023/48/Q/ST1/00048 of the National Science Center, Poland Affiliation: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University Affiliation: Łojasiewicza 6, 30-348, Kraków, Poland Affiliation: &\& Affiliation: Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences Affiliation: Jagiellonian University Affiliation: Łojasiewicza 11, 30-348, Kraków, Poland Email: michal.kudra@doctoral.uj.edu.pl
Abstract

It follows from the Garloff–Wagner Theorem that the set of stable polynomials of degree nn, denoted by ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, i.e., those whose all zeros lie in the left open complex half-plane, with the Hadamard product *, forms an abelian semigroup contained in the abelian group ℝn+\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} of polynomials of degree nn with positive real coefficients. By the idealizer of the set ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, we refer to the largest subsemigroup of ℝn+\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} in which ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} is an ideal. In this paper, we formulate a conjecture characterizing the idealizer of ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} and prove it for n⩽5n\leqslant 5. In addition, we show that the proposed condition is necessary for any polynomial to belong to the idealizer and establish, in a distinguished special case, a sufficient condition of a similar nature that supports the conjecture.

1 Introduction

Let ℝn+\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} denote polynomials of degree nn with positive coefficients. A non-constant polynomial ff of degree nn with real coefficients is called stable if all its zeros lie in the open left half of the complex plane and quasi-stable if all its zeros lie in the closed left half of the complex plane. One of the necessary conditions for stability is that the coefficients of a given polynomial are of the same sign, therefore, for simplicity, when discussing stable polynomials, we only consider the set

ℋn={f∈ℝn+:f⁡(x)=0⇒ℜ⁡(x)<0}.\mathcal{H}_{n}=\left\{f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}:f(x)=0\Rightarrow\Re(x)<0\right\}.

In the case of quasi-stability, we define the set

ℋn⋆={f(x)=∑i=0naixi,ai⩾0(i=1,…,n−1),a0,an>0:f(x)=0⇒ℜ(x)⩽0},\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star}=\left\{f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}x^{i},a_{i}\geqslant 0\;(i=1,\ldots,n-1),\;a_{0},a_{n}>0:f(x)=0\Rightarrow\Re(x)\leqslant 0\right\},

which for the sake of our work represents all quasi-stable polynomials as the assumption a0>0a_{0}>0 does not affect the generality of our reasoning. Details are explained in Subsection 2.3.

It follows from the Garloff–Wagner Theorem [10, Thm. 1] that ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} with the coefficient-wise product ∗\ast, so called the Hadamard product (see Subsection 2.3), is an abelian semigroup in the abelian group ℝn+\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}. Only for n=1,2n=1,2 the semigroup ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} is a group, since ℋ1=ℝ1+\mathcal{H}_{1}=\mathbb{R}_{1}^{+} and ℋ2=ℝ2+\mathcal{H}_{2}=\mathbb{R}_{2}^{+}. For n=3n=3, we see that ℋ3\mathcal{H}_{3} does not contain the identity polynomial 𝕀3\mathbb{I}_{3} with respect to the product ∗\ast, i.e., 𝕀n​(x):=∑j=0nxj\mathbb{I}_{n}(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}x^{j}. We must therefore broaden our perspective to include ℋ3⋆\mathcal{H}_{3}^{\star}, which from the Hermite-Biehler Theorem, is a subset of ℝ3+\mathbb{R}_{3}^{+}. It does indeed contain 𝕀3\mathbb{I}_{3}, but it contains no elements that are inverses of stable polynomials (by the Routh–Hurwitz Theorem). That means it is a commutative monoid, but not a group. However, ℋ4⋆\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\star} cannot be a monoid, since 𝕀4∉ℋ4⋆\mathbb{I}_{4}\notin\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\star}.

For each nn, we seek a maximal subsemigroup Xn⊂ℝn+X_{n}\subset\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} with the Hadamard product ∗\ast, such that ℋn⊂Xn\mathcal{H}_{n}\subset X_{n}, 𝕀n∈Xn\mathbb{I}_{n}\in X_{n}, and for m⩽nm\leqslant\ n

∗:Xn×ℋm→ℋm.\ast:X_{n}\times\mathcal{H}_{m}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{m}. (1)

In other words, we want to characterize

Xn={g∈ℝn+:∀m⩽n,∀f∈ℋmf∗g∈ℋm}={g∈ℝn+:∀m⩽ng∗ℋm⊂ℋm}.X_{n}=\{g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}:\forall m\leqslant n,\;\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{m}\;\;\;f\ast g\in\mathcal{H}_{m}\}=\{g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}:\forall m\leqslant n\;\;\;g\ast\mathcal{H}_{m}\subset\mathcal{H}_{m}\}.

The set XnX_{n} defined this way is the largest submonoid of the group ℝn+\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}, in which ℋm\mathcal{H}_{m} is an ideal. Such a set is called the idealizer of ℋm\mathcal{H}_{m} with respect to the product ∗\ast.

If n=1,2n=1,2, then Xn=ℝn+X_{n}=\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}. It is easy to see that for n=3n=3 we have X3=ℋ3⋆X_{3}=\mathcal{H}_{3}^{\star}. As for n=4n=4, in the paper [5], a family WnW_{n} was introduced for which condition (1) holds in this case. We show that the desired maximal subsemigroup for n=4n=4 is X4=𝒲4¯X_{4}=\overline{\mathcal{W}_{4}}, where 𝒲n¯\overline{\mathcal{W}_{n}} denotes the closure of the set 𝒲n\mathcal{W}_{n} (see Section 4). To our knowledge, no general approach for addressing related problems has yet been established. Available methods seem largely limited in scope, and as some recent papers show, several results have been obtained only for polynomials of degree n⩽5n\leqslant 5 or less (see [2], [3], [4], [5], [15]). After considering the case where n=4n=4, for n≥5n\geq 5, one can suppose that 𝒲n¯\overline{\mathcal{W}_{n}} is a good candidate for the maximal subsemigroup XnX_{n}. However, in Example 1, we show that 𝒲¯5≠X5\overline{\mathcal{W}}_{5}\neq X_{5}. In Section 3, we give a definition of a family of polynomials YnY_{n} for which Y1=ℝ1+=X1Y_{1}=\mathbb{R}_{1}^{+}=X_{1}, Y2=ℝ2+=X2Y_{2}=\mathbb{R}_{2}^{+}=X_{2}, Y3=ℋ3⋆=X3Y_{3}=\mathcal{H}_{3}^{\star}=X_{3}, and Y4=W4¯=X4Y_{4}=\overline{W_{4}}=X_{4} (see Theorem 8). Therefore, we propose the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.

For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, equality Yn=XnY_{n}=X_{n} holds.

The statement is trivial for n=1,2n=1,2, while the case n=3n=3 is readily verified. We prove that Conjecture 1 is true for n=4n=4 (Theorem 8) and n=5n=5 (Theorem 9). Moreover, we show that Xn⊂YnX_{n}\subset Y_{n} for all nn (Theorem 6). We also investigate the idealizer of the set of quasi-stable polynomials. In addition, for a special case, we show a sufficient condition that coincides with Conjecture 1 (Theorem 10).

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the required background from stability theory. We then show necessary conditions for belonging to the idealizer XnX_{n} in Section 3. The main results of the paper are Theorems 8 and 9, presented in Section 4, where we prove that Conjecture 1 is true for n=4n=4 and n=5n=5. Section 5 provides additional information on the idealizer of quasi-stable polynomials, and Section 6 is devoted to supplementary results in a special case, in support of Conjecture 1. Finally, Section 7 provides examples completing our results.

2 Basic definitions and theorems

In the following subsections, we present several characterizations of stability and quasi-stability, and we recall the classical Garloff–Wagner Theorem. These results are extensively used throughout the rest of this paper.

2.1 Stable and quasi-stable polynomials

The Hurwitz matrix of the polynomial f⁡(x)=an​xn+…+a1​x+a0f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\ldots+a_{1}x+a_{0} is defined as

H⁡(f)=[an−1an−3an−5…0anan−2an−4…00an−1an−3…00anan−2…0⋱000…a0],H(f)={\begin{bmatrix}a_{n-1}&a_{n-3}&a_{n-5}&\ldots&0\\ a_{n}&a_{n-2}&a_{n-4}&\ldots&0\\ 0&a_{n-1}&a_{n-3}&\ldots&0\\ 0&a_{n}&a_{n-2}&\ldots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&a_{0}\end{bmatrix}},

and we denote its principal minors by Δk​(f)\Delta_{k}(f). In particular, Δ1​(f)=an−1,Δn​(f)=detH⁡(f)=a0​Δn−1​(f)\Delta_{1}(f)=a_{n-1},\Delta_{n}(f)=\det{H(f)}=a_{0}\Delta_{n-1}(f).

Among the best-known equivalent conditions for stability are the Routh–Hurwitz and Liénard–Chipart Theorems (see [13, Thm. 11.4.5, Thm. 11.4.7]).

Theorem 1 (Routh-Hurwitz).

A polynomial f∈ℝn+f\in\mathbb{R}^{+}_{n} is stable if and only if

Δk​(f)>0​ for all ​k=1,…,n.\Delta_{k}(f)>0\;\textrm{ for all }\;k=1,\ldots,n.
Theorem 2 (Liènard-Chipart).

Given a polynomial f∈ℝn+f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}, the following conditions are equivalent:

    f∈ℋnf\in\mathcal{H}_{n},

  • (ii)

    Δ2(f)>0,Δ4(f)>0,…,Δ2​⌊n/2⌋(f)>0,\Delta_{2}(f)>0,\Delta_{4}(f)>0,\ldots,\Delta_{2\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(f)>0,

In the case of quasi-stable polynomials, it is easy to obtain weak inequalities for the principal minors as the necessary conditions. However, these are not equivalent. They were first formulated in Theorem 4.9 in [1]. By fef_{e} and fof_{o} let us denote even and odd parts of a polynomial ff, such that f⁡(x)=fe​(x2)+x​fo​(x2)f(x)=f_{e}(x^{2})+xf_{o}(x^{2}).

Theorem 3 (Adm, Garloff, Tyaglov).

Given polynomial ff with real coefficients, the following statements are equivalent:

  • (i)

    The polynomial ff belongs to ℋn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} with the stability index m, that is, ff has mm zeros in the open left complex half-plane.

  • (ii)

    The principal minors of the Hurwitz matrix of ff are positive up to order mm, that is

    Δ1​(f)>0,Δ2​(f)>0,…​Δm​(f)>0,Δm+1​(f)=…=Δn​(f)=0\Delta_{1}(f)>0,\;\Delta_{2}(f)>0,\;\ldots\Delta_{m}(f)>0,\;\Delta_{m+1}(f)=\ldots=\Delta_{n}(f)=0

This theorem plays a crucial role in the proofs of Theorem 7 and Lemmas 1 and 2.

2.2 Interlacing and Hermite-Biehler Theorem

Suppose that h∈ℝm+h\in\mathbb{R}_{m}^{+} and g∈ℝn+g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} are polynomials with only real zeros, where those of hh are α1,…,αm\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m}, and those of gg are β1,…,βn\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{n}. We say that gg interlaces hh if either m=n+1m=n+1, and

α1⩽β1⩽α2⩽…⩽βn⩽αn+1\alpha_{1}\leqslant\beta_{1}\leqslant\alpha_{2}\leqslant\ldots\leqslant\beta_{n}\leqslant\alpha_{n+1}

or m=nm=n, and

β1⩽α1⩽β2⩽…⩽βn⩽αn.\beta_{1}\leqslant\alpha_{1}\leqslant\beta_{2}\leqslant\ldots\leqslant\beta_{n}\leqslant\alpha_{n}.

We denote the interlacing property by g≺hg\prec h. Moreover, for any polynomial f∈ℝn+f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+} with only real zeros, we adopt the convention that 0≺f0\prec f and f≺0f\prec 0. We are now ready to formulate the following theorem, which is a slightly simplified version of the Hermite–Biehler Theorem given by Garloff and Wagner, adapted to polynomials from ℋn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} (cf. [10, Thm. 3]).

Theorem 4 (Hermite-Biehler).

Let ff be a polynomial. Then

  • (i)

    f∈ℋn⋆⇔fef\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star}\Leftrightarrow f_{e} and fof_{o} have only negative zeros and fo≺fef_{o}\prec f_{e},

  • (ii)

    f∈ℋn⇔f∈ℋn⋆f\in\mathcal{H}_{n}\Leftrightarrow f\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} and GCD⁡(fe,fo)=1\GCD(f_{e},f_{o})=1,

  • (iii)

    ff has zeros only on the imaginary axis ⇔f∈ℋn⋆\Leftrightarrow f\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} and fo=0f_{o}=0,

  • (iv)

    ff has exactly one zero on the negative half-axis and the rest on the imaginary axis ⇔f∈ℋn⋆,fo≠0\Leftrightarrow f\in\penalty\ \mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star},\;f_{o}\neq 0, and fe=c​fof_{e}=cf_{o}.

The above description of stability and quasi-stability lies at the origin of the family YnY_{n} defined in Section 3.

3 Necessary conditions

When beginning research on any mathematical object, it is often reasonable to consider its behavior in extreme cases. That is an exact idea behind the Pólya-Schur Theorem [13, Thm. 5.7.2], where sequences that are supposed to preserve the reality of polynomial zeros (sometimes called hyperbolicity) are tested solely on polynomials of the form (x+1)n(x+1)^{n}, whose zeros all coincide at the single point. Such so-called multiplier sequences continue to attract interest (see [9], [11], [14]). More generally, there is ongoing research on operators preserving not only the reality of the zeros but also the sectors or strips in which the zeros of a polynomial lie. These operators are reffered to as zero-strip-preserving (or reducing) operators or zero-sector-preserving (or reducing) operators (see [6], [7], [8]). Somewhat surprisingly, these testing polynomials have remained essentially unchallenged. In our setting, in addition to preserving the reality of zeros, we must also account for the interlacing property of the even and odd parts of the polynomial. This additional requirement naturally leads us to introduce the following class of objects that are used throughout this paper.

Polynomials of the form

Qk​(x)=(x2+1)l+x​(x2+1)l for ​k=2​l+1,Q^{k}(x)=(x^{2}+1)^{l}+x(x^{2}+1)^{l}\qquad\textrm{ for }k=2l+1,
Qk​(x)=(x2+1)l for ​k=2​l,Q^{k}(x)=(x^{2}+1)^{l}\qquad\textrm{ for }k=2l,

are called basic quasi-stable polynomials of degree kk, and

Qmk​(x)=xm​Qk​(x) for ​k,m∈ℕ,Q_{m}^{k}(x)=x^{m}Q^{k}(x)\qquad\textrm{ for }k,m\in\mathbb{N},

the mm-shifted basic quasi-stable polynomials of degree kk.

Note that the polynomials QkQ^{k} defined above are special cases of (d)(d) and (c)(c) in the Hermite–Biehler Theorem. Additionally, we define the family of polynomials YnY_{n}, intended to be the idealizer of the set ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, as follows

Yn:={g∈ℝn+:g∗Qmkxm∈ℋk⋆∀k,m∈ℕ, such that k⩾2,k+m⩽n}.Y_{n}:=\left\{g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}:\frac{g*Q_{m}^{k}}{x^{m}}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}^{\star}\;\;\forall k,m\in\mathbb{N},\textrm{ such that }k\geqslant 2,k+m\leqslant n\right\}.

In other words, the family YnY_{n} consists of polynomials such that the Hadamard product of their every k-term sum of consecutive monomials with the basic quasi-stable polynomial belongs to ℋk⋆\mathcal{H}_{k}^{\star}, i.e., polynomials which preserve the quasi-stability of every possible QmkQ^{k}_{m}. We now show that the set YnY_{n} satisfies the necessary condition for belonging to XnX_{n}.

Theorem 6.

Suppose that m⩽n,g∈ℝn+m\leqslant n,\;g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}^{+}. The following implications hold

  • (i)

    f∗g∈ℋm∀f∈ℋm⇒g∈Yn,f\ast g\in\mathcal{H}_{m}\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{m}\Rightarrow g\in Y_{n},

  • (ii)

    f∗g∈ℋm⋆∀f∈ℋm⋆⇒g∈Yn.f\ast g\in\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}\Rightarrow g\in Y_{n}.

Consequently, for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, the idealizer XnX_{n} is included in YnY_{n}.

4 Main results

In the paper [5], for n⩾3n\geqslant 3, the authors define the set

𝒲n={g⁡(x)=∑i=0nbi​xi:bi​bi−1>bi−2​bi+1​(i=2,…,n−1)},\mathcal{W}_{n}=\left\{g(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}x^{i}:b_{i}b_{i-1}>b_{i-2}b_{i+1}\;(i=2,\ldots,n-1)\right\},

which determines the sufficient conditions for the so-called generalized Hadamard product of a polynomial of degree n⩾4n\geqslant 4 with any stable polynomial of degree m⩽4m\leqslant 4 to be stable. As a corollary, we present a special case of this theorem in which we consider the classical Hadamard product of polynomials of degree 44 and mm (cf. [5, Thm. 3.1]).

Corollary 3 (Białas-Góra).

Suppose that m⩽4m\leqslant 4. The following implication holds

g∈𝒲4⇒f∗g∈ℋm∀f∈ℋm.g\in\mathcal{W}_{4}\Rightarrow f\ast g\in\mathcal{H}_{m}\qquad\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{m}.

However, the above implication cannot be reversed. No matter how we choose f∈ℋ4f\in\mathcal{H}_{4}, for g⁡(x)=x4+x3+x2+x+1g(x)=x^{4}+x^{3}+x^{2}+x+1, their product f∗g∈ℋ4f*g\in\mathcal{H}_{4}, but g∉𝒲4g\notin\mathcal{W}_{4}. Therefore, we need another family of polynomials so that the estimates used in the proof can be slightly improved. For n⩾3n\geqslant 3, let us consider the closure of 𝒲n\mathcal{W}_{n}, i.e.,

𝒲n¯={g⁡(x)=∑i=0nbi​xi:bi​bi−1⩾bi−2​bi+1​(i=2,…,n−1)},\overline{\mathcal{W}_{n}}=\left\{g(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}x^{i}:b_{i}b_{i-1}\geqslant b_{i-2}b_{i+1}\;(i=2,\ldots,n-1)\right\},

thanks to which we are able to obtain the following result.

Theorem 7.

Suppose that m⩽4m\leqslant 4. The following implications hold

therefore, 𝒲4¯\overline{\mathcal{W}_{4}} is included in X4X_{4}.

5 The idealizer of the set of quasi-stable polynomials

One might wonder about the idealizer for the set ℋn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star}. Again for each nn we seek a maximal subsemigroup Xn⋆X_{n}^{\star} with the Hadamard product ∗\ast, such that ℋn⋆⊂Xn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star}\subset X_{n}^{\star}, 𝕀n∈Xn⋆\mathbb{I}_{n}\in X_{n}^{\star}, and for m⩽nm\leqslant\ n

∗:Xn⋆×ℋm⋆→ℋm⋆.\ast:X_{n}^{\star}\times\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}.

Since polynomials in ℋn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} may have vanishing coefficients, and ℋn⋆\mathcal{H}_{n}^{\star} has to be a subset of Xn⋆X_{n}^{\star}, we must allow the polynomials from Xn⋆X_{n}^{\star} to also have nonnegative coefficients. Hence

Xn⋆={g(x)=∑i=0nbixi,bi⩾0(i=1,…,n−1),b0,bn>0:∀m⩽n,∀f∈ℋm⋆f∗g∈ℋm⋆}X_{n}^{\star}=\left\{g(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}x^{i},b_{i}\geqslant 0\;(i=1,\ldots,n-1),\;b_{0},b_{n}>0:\forall m\leqslant n,\;\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}\;\;\;f\ast g\in\mathcal{H}_{m}^{\star}\right\}

It is easy to observe that for odd nn, we have Xn=Xn⋆X_{n}=X_{n}^{\star}. Indeed, in this case, the quasi-stable polynomials under consideration have all coefficients positive, and hence (provided that bn,b0>0b_{n},b_{0}>0) all coefficients of any g∈Xn⋆g\in X_{n}^{\star} must also be positive. In contrast, when nn is even, quasi-stable polynomials may have vanishing odd-indexed coefficients. In such cases, they are of the form f⁡(x)=fe​(x2)f(x)=f_{e}(x^{2}), where fef_{e} is a polynomial with only real zeros (by the Hermite–Biehler theorem). To obtain Xn⋆X_{n}^{\star}, it is therefore sufficient to enlarge the set XnX_{n} by including polynomials of the form g⁡(x)=ge​(x2)g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}), where the coefficients of geg_{e}, when combined with those of fef_{e} via the Hadamard product, preserve the reality of zeros. Let Hypn+\Hyp_{n}^{+} denote the class of polynomials of degree nn with only real negative zeros. Then

X2​l⋆=X2​l∪{g(x)=ge(x2),ge∈ℝl+:∀f∈Hypl+ge∗f∈Hypl+}.X_{2l}^{\star}=X_{2l}\cup\left\{g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}),\;g_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{l}^{+}:\forall f\in\Hyp_{l}^{+}\;g_{e}*f\in\Hyp_{l}^{+}\right\}.

In other words, the coefficients of geg_{e} must form a finite multiplier sequence (cf. [14]) preserving Hypl+\Hyp_{l}^{+}. Thus, in the quasi-stable setting, we incorporate a special class of polynomials that highlights the strong connections between the results of this paper and the Pólya-Schur Theorem. Thus

X4⋆=X4∪{g(x)=ge(x2),ge∈ℝ2+:g∗Q4∈ℋ4⋆}==X4∪{g(x)=ge(x2),ge∈ℝ2+:ge(x)∗(x+1)2∈Hyp2+}.X_{4}^{\star}=X_{4}\cup\left\{g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}),\;g_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{2}^{+}:g*Q_{4}\in\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\star}\right\}=\\ =X_{4}\cup\left\{g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}),\;g_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{2}^{+}:g_{e}(x)*(x+1)^{2}\in\Hyp_{2}^{+}\right\}.

In analogy with the previous construction, we set Yn⋆=YnY_{n}^{\star}=Y_{n} for odd nn, while for n=2​ln=2l we define Y2​l⋆Y_{2l}^{\star} as follows

Y2​l⋆:=Y2​l∪{g(x)=ge(x2),ge∈ℝl+:g∗Q2​ν∈ℋ2​ν⋆∀ν∈{2,…,l}}==Y2​l∪{g(x)=ge(x2),ge∈ℝl+:ge(x)∗(x+1)ν∈Hypν+∀ν∈{2,…,l}}.Y_{2l}^{\star}:=Y_{2l}\cup\left\{g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}),\;g_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{l}^{+}:g*Q_{2\nu}\in\mathcal{H}_{2\nu}^{\star}\;\;\forall\;\nu\in\{2,\ldots,l\}\right\}=\\ =Y_{2l}\cup\left\{g(x)=g_{e}(x^{2}),\;g_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{l}^{+}:g_{e}(x)*(x+1)^{\nu}\in\Hyp_{\nu}^{+}\;\;\forall\;\nu\in\{2,\ldots,l\}\right\}.

We therefore formulate the corresponding conjecture for quasi-stable polynomials.

Conjecture 2.

For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, equality Yn⋆=Xn⋆Y_{n}^{\star}=X_{n}^{\star} holds.

6 A special case

We now show a sufficient condition for a special case for all odd nn, which provides the additional rationale behind our hypothesis.

Theorem 10.

Suppose G⁡(x)=g⁡(x2)+x​g​(x2)=(x+1)​g​(x2)G(x)=g(x^{2})+xg(x^{2})=(x+1)g(x^{2}), where g∈ℝk+g\in\mathbb{R}_{k}^{+}. Then the following implication holds

G∗Q2​k+1∈ℋ2​k+1⋆⇒F∗G∈ℋ2​k+1⋆∀F∈ℋ2​k+1⋆.G\ast Q^{2k+1}\in\mathcal{H}_{2k+1}^{\star}\Rightarrow F\ast G\in\mathcal{H}_{2k+1}^{\star}\qquad\forall F\in\mathcal{H}_{2k+1}^{\star}.

First, we require the following auxiliary corollary and theorem (cf. [13, Cor. 5.5.8, Cor. 5.5.10, Thm. 6.3.8]).

Corollary 4.

Let f⁡(x)=∑ν=0paν​xνf(x)=\sum_{\nu=0}^{p}a_{\nu}x^{\nu} be a polynomial of degree p⩾2p\geqslant 2 with only real zeros. Let g⁡(x)=∑ν=0qbν​xνg(x)=\sum_{\nu=0}^{q}b_{\nu}x^{\nu} be a polynomial of degree q⩾2q\geqslant 2, whose non-vanishing zeros are all real and of the same sign. For both polynomials, a possible zero at the origin is assumed to be of order less than m:=min⁡{p,q}m:=\min\{p,q\}. Then, for any integers k⩾−1k\geqslant-1, l⩾−1l\geqslant-1, and n⩾max⁡{p,q}n\geqslant\max\{p,q\}, the polynomial

hk​l:=∑μ=0maμ​bμ(μ!)k​((n−μ)!)l​xμh_{kl}:=\sum_{\mu=0}^{m}\frac{a_{\mu}b_{\mu}}{(\mu!)^{k}((n-\mu)!)^{l}}x^{\mu}

has only real zeros. As a special case, if the zeros of ff are all of the same sign σ\sigma, and those of gg are all of the same sign τ\tau, then, for any integers k⩾−1,l⩾−1k\geqslant-1,l\geqslant-1, and n⩾max⁡{p,q}n\geqslant\max\{p,q\}, the polynomial hk​lh_{kl} has only real zeros, all of them being of sign −σ​τ-\sigma\tau.

Theorem 11 (Hermite-Kakeya).

Let PP and QQ be non-constant polynomials with real coefficients. Then PP and QQ have strictly interlacing zeros if and only if , for all λ,μ∈ℝ\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R} such that λ2+μ2≠0\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}\neq 0, the polynomial R⁡(x):=λ​P​(x)+μ​Q​(x)R(x):=\lambda P(x)+\mu Q(x) has simple, real zeros.

Proof of Theorem 10.

Let us consider a polynomial GG that satisfies the conditions of the theorem. When k=1k=1, then GG is quasi-stable. We consider k⩾2k\geqslant 2. Note that the product G∗Q2​k+1G\ast Q^{2k+1} can be written as

G∗Q2​k+1​(x)=((x+1)​g​(x2))∗((x+1)​(x2+1)k)=(x+1)​(g⁡(x2)∗(x2+1)k).G\ast Q^{2k+1}(x)=((x+1)g(x^{2}))*((x+1)(x^{2}+1)^{k})=(x+1)(g(x^{2})*(x^{2}+1)^{k}).

Since G∗Q2​k+1G\ast Q^{2k+1} is quasi-stable, by the Hermite–Biehler Theorem, g⁡(x)∗(x+1)kg(x)*(x+1)^{k} has only negative zeros. Let F⁡(x)=fe​(x2)+x​fo​(x2)F(x)=f_{e}(x^{2})+xf_{o}(x^{2}). If F∈ℋ2​k+1⋆F\in\mathcal{H}_{2k+1}^{\star}, then, again by the Hermite–Biehler Theorem, fo≺fe​ and ​GCD⁡(fe,fo)=w⁡(x)​ has only negative zeros. f_{o}\prec f_{e}\textrm{ and }\GCD(f_{e},f_{o})=w(x)\textrm{ has only negative zeros. } Let fo~​(x):=fo​(x)w⁡(x)\tilde{f_{o}}(x):=\frac{f_{o}(x)}{w(x)} and fe~​(x):=fe​(x)w⁡(x)\tilde{f_{e}}(x):=\frac{f_{e}(x)}{w(x)}. By applying Theorem 11, we know that the polynomial

H⁡(x)=λ​fo​(x)+μ​fe​(x)=w⁡(x)​(λ​fo~​(x)+μ​fe~​(x))H(x)=\lambda f_{o}(x)+\mu f_{e}(x)=w(x)\left(\lambda\tilde{f_{o}}(x)+\mu\tilde{f_{e}}(x)\right)

has only real zeros for all λ,μ∈ℝ​ such that ​λ2+μ2≠0\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}\textrm{ such that }\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}\neq 0 as

H~​(x)=λ​fo~​(x)+μ​fe~​(x)\tilde{H}(x)=\lambda\tilde{f_{o}}(x)+\mu\tilde{f_{e}}(x)

has only simple, real zeros for all λ,μ∈ℝ​ such that ​λ2+μ2≠0\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}\textrm{ such that }\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}\neq 0. In turn, from Corollary 4, we know that since g∗(x+1)kg*(x+1)^{k} has negative roots, the polynomial

(H∗g)​(x)=(λ​fo​(x)+μ​fe​(x))∗g⁡(x)=λ​fo∗g⁡(x)+μ​fe∗g⁡(x)\left(H*g\right)(x)=(\lambda f_{o}(x)+\mu f_{e}(x))*g(x)=\lambda f_{o}*g(x)+\mu f_{e}*g(x)

has only real zeros for all λ,μ∈ℝ​ such that ​λ2+μ2≠0\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}\textrm{ such that }\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}\neq 0. Let us denote the common multiple zeros of fo∗gf_{o}*g and fe∗gf_{e}*g as ξi​(i=0,…,m)\xi_{i}\;(i=0,\ldots,m), where m⩽km\leqslant k. If m=km=k, then fo∗g=fe∗gf_{o}*g=f_{e}*g, which have negative zeros (from Corollary 4), and the polynomial F∗GF*G is quasi-stable. If, however, m<km<k then

(H∗g)​(x)=∑i=0m(x−ξi)​(λ​fo∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi)+μ​fe∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi)).(H*g)(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})\left(\lambda\frac{f_{o}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})}+\mu\frac{f_{e}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})}\right).

Thus, we obtain that the polynomial

λ​fo∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi)+μ​fe∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi)\lambda\frac{f_{o}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})}+\mu\frac{f_{e}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})}

has simple, real zeros for all λ,μ∈ℝ​ such that ​λ2+μ2≠0\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}\textrm{ such that }\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}\neq 0. We conclude that

fo∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi)≺fe∗g⁡(x)∑i=0m(x−ξi),\frac{f_{o}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})}\prec\frac{f_{e}*g(x)}{\sum_{i=0}^{m}(x-\xi_{i})},

and therefore that

fo∗g≺fe∗g.f_{o}*g\prec f_{e}*g.

Again, by Corollary 4, the zeros of fo∗gf_{o}*g and fe∗gf_{e}*g are negative, which completes the proof. ∎

Unfortunately, to the best of our knowledge, in this case, there are no available tools for determining the stability of F∗GF*G, even under the assumption that FF is stable.
